topic: reasoning and agents; formal deduction; language-model reasoning benchmarks
status: bounded synthesis of 11 new random-frame full-text audits plus one earlier frame audit; testable evaluation hypothesis, not field prevalence or general model ranking
claim: In this small fixed-frame slice, reported success depends strongly on what is scored: FLD reports large gaps between correct answers and valid proofs; RegexPSPACE separates equivalence decisions from minimal constructions; CoT-decoding improves benchmark answer accuracy but does not establish chain faithfulness and incurs extra inference. This supports testing whether answer-only metrics overstate reliable reasoning artifacts on tasks where traces/proofs can be checked. It does not imply every reasoning task needs a textual chain: BRUE evaluates the action choice it targets, and the human–robot study measures team behavior and participant ratings.
positive_evidence: On FLD, GPT-4 answer/proof accuracy is 52.4%/12.8%; on FLD-star it is 49.4%/3.2%.
On RegexPSPACE, GPT-OSS-low has 84.45% equivalence, 67.36% minimality, and 78.48% output-length ratio; these are distinct outcomes.
CoT-decoding raises pretrained Mistral-7B GSM8K accuracy to 25.1% from 9.9% greedy in the reported setup, while the paper also records state-tracking/arithmetic errors and extra decoding work.
counterevidence: BRUE evaluates simple regret and action-selection error, directly measuring the decision the planner is intended to improve rather than a verbal rationale.
The human–robot work measures elapsed time, task allocation, and subjective ratings, so behavioral outcomes can complement internal traces.
FLD includes transfer to human-authored EntailmentBank, although that result remains within a constrained deductive task and required full target-example training.
falsifiable_test: On several tasks with independently machine-checkable proofs, plans, or traces, compare answer-only, answer-plus-self-reported-rationale, and answer-plus-verified-artifact systems at matched model family and compute/token budgets. Use held-out templates, increasing proof depth, independent verifiers, and downstream execution outcomes. The hypothesis is weakened if answer accuracy alone predicts verified-artifact validity and held-out task success just as well at matched cost, or if verifier checks add no decision value.
limitations: Evidence combines unlike tasks and models across 2012–2025; it cannot estimate how often answer scores overstate reasoning across all CS or establish a single best metric.

topic: human-robot collaboration; multimodal model selection; medical QA routing
status: bounded synthesis of three random-frame full-text audits; falsifiable evaluation hypothesis, not causal meta-analysis or clinical claim
claim: Adaptivity and specialist routing can improve selected outcomes, but benchmark gains are conditional on what enters evaluation and what counts as success. In virtual human–robot collaboration, adaptive policies improve speed/preference while one task-allocation expectation is contradicted and human motion is scripted. M³ reports selector gains after filtering invalid generated computation graphs and remains below an oracle. MedRouter reports modest mean QA improvements over routing baselines but has a large per-question oracle gap and uses an LLM judge. The supported claim is complementarity worth testing—not that routing inherently improves reliability or real-world outcomes.
positive_evidence: The human–robot study reports faster completion and higher participant preference for more adaptive virtual robots.
M³ reports about 69% successful execution versus about 56% random selection on its filtered MS-GQA examples.
MedRouter reports 45.9%/46.1% mean accuracy across two answer generators versus 42.6% for its strongest compared router on eight QA benchmarks.
counterevidence: The human–robot Bayesian-predictive robot completed 1.7 more tasks than the oracle in a small 39-task one-agent comparison, contrary to the direction expected by the task-allocation hypothesis.
M³ filters invalid LLM-generated computation graphs, and its approximately 69% result remains far below a 100% per-example oracle.
MedRouter's reported per-question oracle is 64.3%, well above its achieved mean, and GPT-5.6-luna judges answer correctness; none of these results establishes clinical safety.
falsifiable_test: Compare adaptive/routed policies against fixed and oracle policies on preregistered held-out task families. Count failures before routing (including task decomposition), end-to-end success, subgroup/task-specific errors, model calls, latency and cost; independently verify outcomes, and include human preference only where relevant. The hypothesis is weakened if gains vanish after invalid cases and resource costs are counted or fail to transfer beyond tuned benchmarks.
limitations: Three heterogeneous studies do not support prevalence estimates. One is simulated human–robot interaction, one is a single filtered multimodal benchmark, and one is medical QA research judged by an LLM rather than clinical deployment.

status: hypothesis prompted by one 2026 survey audit; not an exhaustive review or novelty claim
claim: A 2026 survey curates 135 secure-RAG works and reports that 14 of 15 evaluation-primary studies mainly target fixed queries/instances, with one centered on cross-query targets; it argues there is no unified defense-aware harness spanning pipeline surfaces. The survey also acknowledges multi-surface studies, so the defensible opportunity is to test whether integrating cross-query and multi-surface attacks/defenses under one comparable protocol changes defense rankings or reveals failure propagation—not to claim multi-surface evaluation does not exist.
positive_evidence: The survey's mapped evaluation-primary set is skewed toward fixed-instance targets (14/15), while aggregate/cross-query testing is central in one study.
It notes that metrics such as attack success, stance shift, and certification are not directly rankable when threat assumptions and evaluation setups differ.
counterevidence: The survey explicitly recognizes existing multi-surface studies including SafeRAG, OpenRAG-Soc, and Rag’n Roll.
A proposed common harness may add little if existing studies already cover the relevant threat surfaces or if a shared protocol does not alter conclusions.
The paper is a snapshot through 2026-04-30 and uses screening/selection choices that can miss work.
falsifiable_test: Implement a common, defense-aware harness over a preregistered set of retrieval, indexing, query, and cross-query attack surfaces. Run representative existing defenses under matched threat models, budgets, corpora, and outcome definitions; measure attack success, utility/stance shift, cross-query leakage, failure propagation, cost, and ranking stability. The opportunity is weakened if existing evaluations already yield comparable rankings and the common harness exposes no additional failures or reproducibility gains.
limitations: One survey is not a full systematic replication and its 15 evaluation-primary studies are a subset of its 135 curated works. No harness was implemented or executed in this literature audit; the gap is a candidate research direction, not confirmed novelty.
